newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian nuclear power plan put on hold.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian nuclear power plan put on hold.

text.p: A mixture of economics and politics apparently prompted Indonesia to delay plans to build its first nuclear power station for another 20 or 30 years, analysts said on Thursday.
"The project does not appear to be viable," one Jakarta-based analyst, who has watched Indonesia's nuclear power plans closely, told Reuters.
Indonesia's flamboyant minister for research and technology, Jusuf Habibie, had vigorously pushed the nuclear power project through the National Atomic Energy Body (BATAN) which he oversees.

But in typically unscripted remarks, he told a Jakarta energy conference on Tuesday: "Maybe we will finally need a nuclear power station in 2020 or 2030. Now we have an excess supply of electricity. Because of that our energy needs need to be revised again."
Diplomats said Habibie's comments could reflect a wind of change in government policy which had not yet been formalised.
"There is no doubt it came from the top, but Habibie's comments reflect a conversation he may have had rather than any formal written government decision," a diplomat said.
The nuclear analyst, who asked not to be identified, said the $7 billion nuclear power station project was too expensive for Indonesia. The project has also come under fire from environmentalists.
Indonesia has extensive reserves of oil, natural gas and coal, but little uranium.

BATAN had said the government planned to start building a 7,200 megawatt nuclear power station with foreign help at Mount Muria in central Java in 1998 or 1999 pending the results of a feasiblity study. The plant was due to start operating by 2003.

Analysts said the state power utility Perusahaan Listrik Negara (PLN) was strongly criticised when in 1995 it signed a landmark deal to buy power at 8.56 cents per kilowatt hour from the first private power plant, the $2.5 billion coal-fired Paiton project.
They said local people feared high power costs would be passed on to Indonesia's 200 million heavily subsidised consumers whose average annual income is only around $1,000.
Last November, PLN signed two more private power contracts at the lower rates of 5.76 cents and 6.09 cents per kilowatt hour.

"If PLN faced an outcry for its power-sharing agreement with Paiton, then what's going to happen if they have to buy electricty from a nuclear power station at the estimated cost of 12 cents per kilowatt hour?," one analyst asked.
PLN faces significant difficulties financing its much needed expansion programme and the utility is currently under an organisational review ahead of its possible privatisation.
"One of the things they must be looking at is how to privatise it without having any more high-priced power agreements," the analyst said.
Mohammad Anung from the Indonesian Anti-Nuclear Society (MANI) was sceptical about any formal change in policy.

"I'm doubtful about the government's statement because the newly endorsed (nuclear energy) bill does not say anything about nuclear energy as the last power supply alternative," Anung was quoted as saying.
"I'm afraid the statement was just a government move to appease nuclear protestors," he said.
